Double Poisson Distribution

Source: R/dpo.R
DoublePoisson.Rd

Density, distribution function, quantile function, and random generation for the double Poisson distribution of Efron (1986), normalized exactly.

Usage

ddpo(x, lambda, phi, log = FALSE)

pdpo(q, lambda, phi, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

qdpo(p, lambda, phi, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

rdpo(n, lambda, phi)

Arguments

x

vector of (non-negative integer) quantiles.

lambda

vector of (positive) location parameters \(\lambda\).

phi

vector of (positive) precision parameters \(\phi\). \(\phi = 1\) is the Poisson distribution, \(\phi < 1\) gives overdispersion and \(\phi > 1\) underdispersion.

log, log.p

logical; if TRUE, probabilities p are given as log(p).

q

vector of quantiles.

lower.tail

logical; if TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(Y \leq y)\), otherwise \(P(Y > y)\).

p

vector of probabilities.

n

number of observations. If length(n) > 1, the length is taken to be the number required.

Value

ddpo gives the probability mass, pdpo the distribution function, qdpo the quantile function, and rdpo random deviates. The length of the result is determined by n for rdpo, and is the maximum of the lengths of the numerical arguments for the other functions.

Details

The double Poisson distribution has probabilities proportional to the weights (with \(0 \log 0 = 0\)) $$w(y) = \exp\left\{\phi y \log\lambda + (1 - \phi) y \log y + (\phi - 1) y - \log y!\right\}, \quad y = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$ which is Efron's (1986) expression with the factors that do not depend on \(y\) removed. Here the normalizing constant \(\sum_{j \geq 0} w(j)\) is computed numerically (by summing the weights around their mode until the remaining tail, bounded by a geometric series, is negligible), so the probabilities sum to one. Efron's closed-form approximation of the constant is not used: it is least accurate for small \(\lambda\) and strong dispersion.

\(\lambda\) is a location parameter: the mean is close to, but not exactly, \(\lambda\), and the variance is approximately \(\lambda / \phi\). The exact moments are computed from the normalized probabilities when needed. Some references (e.g. the DPO family of gamlss.dist) use the dispersion \(\sigma = 1 / \phi\) instead of the precision.

Upper tail probabilities (lower.tail = FALSE) are summed directly, never computed as one minus the distribution function. rdpo() uses inversion of the distribution function.

References

Efron, B. (1986). Double exponential families and their use in generalized linear regression. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 81(395), 709-721.

Examples

ddpo(0:6, lambda = 3, phi = 0.5)
#> [1] 0.15271589 0.16043444 0.16854311 0.15333984 0.12400709 0.09103218 0.06158654
# phi = 1 gives the Poisson distribution
all.equal(ddpo(0:10, lambda = 3, phi = 1), dpois(0:10, 3))
#> [1] TRUE
sum(ddpo(0:200, lambda = 3, phi = 2.5))   # exactly normalized
#> [1] 1
pdpo(c(2, 5), lambda = 3, phi = 2.5)
#> [1] 0.3353030 0.9835871
qdpo(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), lambda = 3, phi = 0.5)
#> [1] 0 3 6
set.seed(2)
y <- rdpo(2000, lambda = 5, phi = 3)
c(mean = mean(y), var = var(y))   # underdispersed
#>     mean      var 
#> 5.016000 1.775632
